A separate 30-request crossover shows that graph structure changes 16 decisions and improves the paired penalized score, while a depth-1 stump matches gradient boosting. The evidence supports resource-aware representation selection at n <= 35, p <= 5, with gains driven by representation features rather than classifier complexity.
tldr: This paper introduces RASP-QAOA, a per-instance selector for choosing among ten computational representations for exact QAOA simulation, focusing on resource-aware selection.
motivation: Exact QAOA simulation performance varies significantly across representations depending on graph structure, circuit depth, precision, and memory, and choosing only a backend name hides these differences.
method: RASP-QAOA filters out inadmissible actions, then ranks remaining actions using instance features, with analytical work estimates for out-of-support cases.
result: On a 60-request evaluation, RASP-QAOA achieves 27/31 top-1 and 31/31 top-2 selection with low regret, and outperforms a baseline in failure-penalized score.
conclusion: The results support resource-aware representation selection for QAOA simulation, with gains driven by representation features rather than classifier complexity.

title: On The Figures Of Merit For Quantum Software Security: Toward A Benchmarking Rubric
authors: Badhon Rahman, Majid Haghparast, Tommi Mikkonen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum software is increasingly provided through multi-tenant and cloud-based Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) stacks. A growing concern about the diverse attack vectors across the pipeline has been demonstrated in recent research. Yet the community has converged on three mature pillars: Scale (Qubit Count), Quality (Quantum Volume), and Speed (Circuit Layer Operations per Second (CLOPS)) for the merit performance figures. Moreover, it has also begun to define software-quality metrics. However, the security of quantum software remains largely unmeasured. A few quantitative security indicators, such as Total Variation Distance (TVD) and Degree of Functional Corruption (DFC), exist. Although they were introduced ad hoc for individual circuit obfuscation techniques, they are incompatible. We assert that the security of quantum software deserves the same attention as the performance: an explicit set of Security Figures of Merit (S-FoMs). The research of this paper is threefold: (i) characterizes a three-layer measurement gap, (ii) proposes a structured S-FoM set organized by ISO/IEC 25010 security sub-characteristics, QaaS pipeline mapping, and measurement maturity, and (iii) defines a benchmarking rubric that normalizes and aggregates S-FoMs into a combined Quantum Software Security Posture (QSSP) score. Additionally, an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques has been presented. Our aim is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the Quantum Software Stack (QSS).
tldr: This paper proposes a benchmarking rubric for quantum software security, focusing on security figures of merit rather than quantum information theory or physics.
motivation: Quantum software security is largely unmeasured, and existing metrics are ad hoc and incompatible, so the authors aim to establish a structured set of security figures of merit.
method: The authors characterize a three-layer measurement gap, propose a structured S-FoM set based on ISO/IEC 25010, and define a rubric that aggregates S-FoMs into a Quantum Software Security Posture score.
result: They present an illustrative reanalysis of published obfuscation techniques to demonstrate the rubric's application.
conclusion: The work is a first step toward security-aware benchmarking of the quantum software stack, but it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: An End-to-End Threat Model For The Quantum-as-a-Service Pipeline
authors: Badhon Rahman, Majid Haghparast, Tommi Mikkonen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud-based accessing of Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) platforms such as IBM Quantum, IonQ Cloud, and Amazon Braket is becoming popular day by day. Hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QML) transfer data via a long layered pipeline of orchestration, compilation, and execution. Recent works have demonstrated various critical attacks at individual stages: Calibration tampering, SWAP attacks, QubitHammer, and so on. However, these attacks remain separated because of their own terminology, and existing STRIDE-based threat modeling in the context of quantum lacks a structured view towards the QaaS stack itself. We address this concern by decomposing the workflow into six-stage model with STRIDE threat modeling. Our matrix demonstrated attack vectors in quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible tiers for each of the stages. We further investigate the underexplored sections (repudiation and elevation-of-privilege) and distinguish three different cross-stage attack chains with higher impacts.
tldr: This paper proposes a STRIDE-based threat model for the Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) pipeline, decomposing the workflow into six stages and analyzing attack vectors.
motivation: Existing security analyses of QaaS platforms are fragmented, lacking a structured view of the entire pipeline. The authors aim to provide a comprehensive threat model to identify and categorize vulnerabilities.
method: The authors decompose the QaaS workflow into six stages and apply STRIDE threat modeling to each, creating a matrix of attack vectors. They also investigate underexplored threat categories and identify cross-stage attack chains.
result: The paper presents a structured threat model with a matrix of attack vectors across stages, highlighting quantum-specific, inherited classical, and plausible threats. It also identifies three cross-stage attack chains with higher impact.
conclusion: The proposed threat model provides a systematic framework for understanding and mitigating security risks in QaaS pipelines, though it is not directly aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information theory, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Multiphysics Tritium Transport Modelling Of The Arc Breeding Blanket With Festim
authors: James Dark, Arpan Sircar, Jin Whan Bae, J{\o}rgen S. Dokken, R\'emi Delaporte-Mathurin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of tritium behaviour in molten salt breeding blankets is essential for the design and safe operation of ARC-class fusion reactors. This work presents a fully open-source, component-scale multiphysics framework for modelling tritium transport in an ARC liquid immersion blanket. Neutron transport, thermal hydraulics, and hydrogen isotope transport are coupled using OpenMC, OpenFOAM, and FESTIM, leveraging dedicated tools enabling direct transfer of spatially resolved fields between solvers. Assuming a zero inlet concentration, steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of approximately 243 mg, with the blanket reaching steady-state tritium throughput within approximately 30 min, which is of a similar order to previous system-level estimates. The results show that tritium transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion, with strong localisation in flow stagnation regions and reduced accumulation in highly turbulent zones. Sensitivity analyses indicate that predicted inventories are governed primarily by the numerical stabilisation scheme, with only a modest dependence on the turbulent Schmidt number. The proposed workflow provides a transparent and extensible basis for high-fidelity analysis of tritium transport in ARC-class breeding blankets.
tldr: This paper presents a multiphysics simulation framework for tritium transport in a fusion breeding blanket, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Accurate prediction of tritium behavior is essential for the design and safety of fusion reactors, but this topic is outside the scope of the user's specified research directions.
method: The authors couple neutron transport (OpenMC), thermal hydraulics (OpenFOAM), and hydrogen isotope transport (FESTIM) in a component-scale model of an ARC liquid immersion blanket.
result: Steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of ~243 mg, with steady-state throughput reached in ~30 min, and show that transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion with sensitivity to numerical stabilization.
conclusion: The proposed workflow provides a transparent basis for tritium transport analysis in fusion blankets, but it has no connection to quantum information science or related fields.

title: Inverse Mask Design For Interference Lithography Using Automatic Differentiable Wave Propagation
authors: Chuntian Cao, Jangwoon Sung, Jack Griffiths, Yuan Gao, Xi Yu, Paul Baity, Nikhil Tiwale, Zhitian Shi, Juhong Ahn, Shinjae Yoo, Yong S. Chu, Chang-Yong Nam
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interference lithography (IL) is powerful for fabricating high-resolution periodic nanostructures, but designing masks to produce non-periodic patterns remains challenging. We introduce a gradient-based optimization framework for binary IL mask design using automatic differentiation. The forward model is implemented using the differentiable angular spectrum method (ASM). The inverse mask design is formulated as an optimization problem, where the mask logits are updated through backpropagation of the loss between the simulated field amplitude and the target pattern. We optimize a mask that reproduces a target pattern with only 0.1% isolated pixel-level defects, resolving features at half the mask pixel pitch. To scale mask optimization, we employ the shifted ASM, which partitions the mask into patches that are propagated independently and summed at the image plane. For a 3.84 mm[MATH]3.84 mm mask, shifted ASM with 16 patches reduces peak GPU memory by 3.8[MATH] at only 1.3[MATH] runtime cost relative to standard ASM. With gradient checkpointing, peak memory is reduced by 7.4[MATH] at 2[MATH] runtime. Distributing across multiple GPUs further accelerates the optimization. This work establishes a physics-informed, machine learning-driven approach for IL mask design, moving a step further towards complex, non-periodic patterns. The source code is available at [URL] .
tldr: This paper presents a gradient-based optimization framework for binary interference lithography mask design using automatic differentiation and differentiable angular spectrum method.
motivation: Interference lithography is powerful for periodic nanostructures, but designing masks for non-periodic patterns is challenging.
method: The authors formulate inverse mask design as an optimization problem, updating mask logits via backpropagation of the loss between simulated field amplitude and target pattern, and use shifted ASM for scalability.
result: The method achieves 0.1% pixel-level defects, resolves features at half the mask pixel pitch, and reduces GPU memory by up to 7.4x with gradient checkpointing.
conclusion: This work establishes a physics-informed, machine learning-driven approach for IL mask design, enabling complex non-periodic patterns.

title: Subexponential Bohnenblust-Hille Inequalities On Finite Cyclic Groups
authors: Anselmo Raposo Jr Daniel M. Pellegrino
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slote, Volberg and Zhang proved a dimension-free Bohnenblust--Hille inequality on products of finite cyclic groups for functions of bounded total degree. Later, Becker, Klein, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proved [MATH] and asked whether the optimal constants are subexponential in the degree. More recently, Defant, Galicer, Mansilla, Masty\l o and Muro established an exponential Bohnenblust--Hille estimate for the larger support-sensitive class governed by the number of active coordinates. We prove that the optimal constants for this larger class grow subexponentially. More precisely, if [MATH] denotes the optimal constant for functions on [MATH] whose Fourier characters involve at most [MATH] coordinates, with no restriction on the nonzero local frequencies, then, for every fixed [MATH], \[ {q}\leq \exp\left(c_q +O_q\left(}\log\log d\right)\right) \qquad(d\to\infty), \] where [MATH] and [MATH] for [MATH]. Since bounded total degree implies bounded interaction order, this also answers the question of Becker et al. The proof uses Potts hypercontractivity, Blei's mixed-norm inequality, orbit counting, and a mixed polarization estimate.
tldr: This paper proves subexponential bounds for Bohnenblust-Hille inequalities on finite cyclic groups, a topic in harmonic analysis and functional analysis.
motivation: The paper addresses an open question about optimal constants in Bohnenblust-Hille inequalities, which have applications in various areas of analysis.
method: The proof uses Potts hypercontractivity, Blei's mixed-norm inequality, orbit counting, and a mixed polarization estimate.
result: The authors show that the optimal constants for the support-sensitive class grow subexponentially in the degree, answering a question by Becker et al.
conclusion: The result provides a subexponential bound for a larger class of functions, improving on previous exponential estimates.

title: The Hidden Life Of Public Safety Communications Signals: A Comparative Security Analysis Of Tetra, Tetrapol, And P25
authors: Sergey Bratus Larry Hernandez
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public-safety agencies and critical infrastructure operators rely on trunked land-mobile radio (LMR) systems, based on P25, TETRA, and TETRAPOL. These systems are expected to protect not just the content of a communication but the fact of it. Yet LMR standards leave a stark gap between confidentiality of and of : underneath an encrypted traffic plane, their signaling plane is almost entirely in the clear. We probe the depth and impact of adversarial inference from this exposed signaling. Prior security analyses of these systems have concentrated on the content plane---recovering encryption keys or capturing accidental cleartext. We show that comparably sensitive information can be . In particular, we show that across the trunked LMR standards, a passive, receive-only software-defined radio (SDR) observer can recover operationally sensitive network topology and geography details, unit presence, mobility across cells and groups, organizational structure, as well as operational security details such as special key domains and key-epoch rotation. This signaling-plane inference reaches far beyond the observer's direct area of reception, turning sniffing into network mapping capabilities that degrade or defeat LMR standards' identity obfuscation through timing and association. In the case of TETRAPOL, we demonstrate how inference and tracking of such signaling metadata and a standards-level confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enable unencrypted voice extraction. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and mitigations, including specific recommendations for protecting inter-cell, base station and subscriber identities.
tldr: This paper analyzes security vulnerabilities in public safety radio standards (TETRA, TETRAPOL, P25) by exploiting exposed signaling metadata to infer sensitive operational information.
motivation: Public safety agencies rely on these systems for confidentiality, but prior analyses focused on content encryption, leaving signaling-plane metadata unprotected and exploitable.
method: The authors conduct a comparative security analysis of the signaling planes of TETRA, TETRAPOL, and P25, demonstrating how a passive SDR observer can recover network topology, unit presence, and other operational details.
result: They show that signaling metadata can be used to map networks and track units, and in TETRAPOL, a confidentiality failure in emergency call handling enables unencrypted voice extraction.
conclusion: The paper recommends countermeasures to protect inter-cell, base station, and subscriber identities, highlighting the need for signaling-plane security in LMR systems.

title: Towards A Characterization Of Counting And Alternating Classes Via Discrete Ordinary Differential Equations
authors: Eduardo Skapinakis Melissa Antonelli
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a high-level report on an ongoing project aiming to leverage implicit approaches based on discrete ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to study multiple complexity classes, even beyond small circuit and polynomial-time classes. Stimulated by recent ODE-based characterizations of polynomial-time functions (FP) and classes over the reals, the research project outlined here pushes this investigation further into counting and alternation. Specifically, we present a uniform framework, built upon a single base algebra and a unified family of schemas, where complexity levels, such as those of the polynomial and counting hierarchies, are captured simply by the nesting depth of ODE operators. Crucially, our approach starts from a base class much weaker than FP, thus strengthening existing recursion-theoretic treatments and establishing a natural connection to descriptive complexity. Moreover, by isolating three elementary schemas, our framework makes the computational content of linearity restrictions completely transparent while extending ODE-based implicit complexity to previously unaddressed counting classes, such as oplusP. More generally, this work establishes a clear bridge between differentiation and counting, offering a fresh perspective on the relationships between different complexity classes, which remains the object of ongoing and future research.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework using discrete ordinary differential equations to characterize counting and alternating complexity classes, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to extend implicit complexity approaches based on ODEs to counting and alternating classes, building on recent characterizations of polynomial-time functions.
method: They present a uniform framework with a single base algebra and a family of schemas, where complexity levels are captured by nesting depth of ODE operators, starting from a base class weaker than FP.
result: The framework captures polynomial and counting hierarchies, extends to classes like ⊕P, and clarifies the role of linearity restrictions.
conclusion: The work establishes a bridge between differentiation and counting, offering new perspectives on complexity class relationships, but it is purely theoretical computer science.

title: Nucleation Beyond Equilibrium: Fronts Control Invasion In Bistable Ecosystems
authors: Victor Lequin, Giulio Biroli, Camille Scalliet
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bistability, the existence of two alternative stable states with distinct basins of attraction, is common across ecology and many other biological, chemical, and physical systems. In spatially extended systems, the invasion of one state by the other proceeds through nucleation, the fluctuation-driven growth of a droplet beyond a critical size. Classical Nucleation Theory (CNT) quantifies this process using the energy landscape, but this description relies on detailed balance, the condition of microscopic reversibility that holds at equilibrium. Ecological dynamics generally violate detailed balance and are described not by a single scalar field but by several coupled, non-conserved abundances--a vector order parameter--for which no general nucleation theory exists. Here we derive such a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, valid both close to the binodal, where invasion proceeds through propagating fronts, and close to the spinodal, where the metastable state loses stability. Extensive numerical computations of the quasipotential confirm the theory in both regimes. We show that the mathematical structure of CNT survives out of equilibrium, once energetic quantities are replaced by dynamical properties of fronts: the front speed plays the role of the bulk free-energy difference between phases, and the diffusivity that of the surface tension. Applied to the two-species Lotka-Volterra model, an archetypal system of bistable ecological antagonism, our theory shows that strong interspecific competition generates a pronounced depletion region within fronts, where the total abundance falls well below carrying capacity. This vectorial structure, invisible to a scalar description based on species frequency alone, makes invasion exponentially harder as competition strengthens at fixed competitive advantage--a prediction testable in microbial systems.
tldr: This paper develops a nucleation theory for bistable ecosystems with non-conserved vector order parameters, showing that front dynamics control invasion beyond equilibrium.
motivation: Classical nucleation theory relies on detailed balance, which ecological systems violate; there is no general theory for vector order parameters.
method: The authors derive a theory for reaction-diffusion systems with a non-conserved vector order parameter, using quasipotential computations and front properties.
result: They show that front speed and diffusivity replace free-energy difference and surface tension, and that strong competition creates depletion regions making invasion exponentially harder.
conclusion: The theory extends nucleation concepts to non-equilibrium ecological systems and provides testable predictions for microbial systems.

title: Superfluid Helium
authors: Charles Radin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We are interested in modelling superfluid helium-4, the common isotope of helium, of atomic number 4. We present a mathematically solvable toy model of the phase transition between the normal liquid and superfluid phases and use it to show how an order parameter might be obtained for the superfluid.
tldr: This paper presents a toy model for the superfluid phase transition in helium-4, focusing on mathematical modeling rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to model superfluid helium-4 and demonstrate how an order parameter can be obtained for the superfluid phase transition.
method: They introduce a mathematically solvable toy model of the phase transition between normal liquid and superfluid phases.
result: The model shows how an order parameter might be obtained for the superfluid.
conclusion: The paper contributes to condensed matter physics but does not align with the specified research directions.

title: Incidence-based Combinatorial Geometry On Cell Complexes
authors: Andrey P. Jivkov, Muhammad Azeem, Aneirin Griffiths, Pieter D. Boom
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial Mesh Calculus (CMC) formulates conservation laws directly on cell complexes using combinatorial differential forms and their cochain representations. This note develops an incidence-based geometric extension of that framework for directional quantities and local geometric structure on explicit cellular organisation. The central construction is a family of local fibres generated intrinsically by the incidence structure of the complex. Each vertex carries a vector space spanned by its incident edge directions, providing a combinatorial analogue of a tangent space whose dimension reflects local topology. These fibres define local coefficient spaces for incidence-based vector-, covector- and endomorphism-valued cochains. Directed transport maps compare states attached to neighbouring fibres, while a canonical solder form relates fibre directions to the underlying cell-complex structure. Together they give rise to finite combinatorial analogues of transport, torsion, curvature and metric structure. Evaluation cup products provide pairings between kinematic and force-like quantities, while bundle Hodge operators induced by the fibre metric relate vector- and covector-valued cochains, and weighted covariant incidence operators define degree-raising transport-corrected operations on incidence cochains. The framework does not assume a smooth manifold, fixed-rank bundle, cellular sheaf or local system. Instead, geometric structure is generated directly from the organisation represented by the cell complex. The resulting theory establishes a combinatorial scaffold for geometry on explicit cellular organisation and identifies the principal mathematical questions required for its further development, including admissible transport classes, metric compatibility, Cartan-type structure equations and locality-dependent algebraic structures.
tldr: This paper develops a combinatorial geometric framework on cell complexes using incidence structures, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to extend combinatorial mesh calculus to handle directional quantities and local geometry on discrete cellular structures without assuming a smooth manifold.
method: They construct local fibres from incidence structure, define incidence-based cochains, directed transport maps, solder forms, and bundle Hodge operators, leading to combinatorial analogues of curvature and metric.
result: The framework provides a combinatorial scaffold for geometry on cell complexes, with potential applications in computational physics and topology.
conclusion: The paper establishes foundational mathematical structures but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Persistence Of Invariant Graphs For Twist Maps Under Analytic Perturbations
authors: Qi Li, Yi Liu, Lin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the persistence for invariant graphs of twist maps that exhibit the strongest possible dynamics, namely those real-analytically conjugate to rigid rotations, under Gevrey-[MATH] ([MATH]) perturbations. By enhancing the regularity of the perturbation itself, we show that invariant graphs with the strongest dynamics can persist even when the size of the perturbation and the constraints on the frequency go beyond the requirements of classical KAM theory and the theory of normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds. The proofs of these results are based on a parameterized direct KAM method.
tldr: This paper studies persistence of invariant graphs for twist maps under Gevrey perturbations using a parameterized direct KAM method.
motivation: The authors aim to extend classical KAM theory to show that invariant graphs with strongest dynamics can persist under more general perturbations and frequency constraints.
method: They employ a parameterized direct KAM method, enhancing the regularity of the perturbation to prove persistence results.
result: They demonstrate that invariant graphs with the strongest dynamics persist even when perturbation size and frequency constraints exceed classical KAM and normally hyperbolic invariant manifold requirements.
conclusion: The work contributes to dynamical systems theory, specifically KAM theory, but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: A Variational Framework For Bayesian Inversion In Moving Boundary Darcy Flow
authors: Michael E. Causon, Marco A. Iglesias, Michael V. Tretyakov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an infinite-dimensional Bayesian framework for recovering spatially varying log-permeability from pressure observations in single-phase Darcy flow with a moving boundary, motivated by resin transfer moulding. The main contribution is an observation-wise representer formulation linking sensitivities of the parameter-to-observable map to the moving-boundary state and adjoint systems. This yields a reduced Levenberg--Marquardt method for maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation on the Cameron--Martin space of a Gaussian prior and an explicit finite-rank covariance for the linearised MAP (LMAP) approximation. Once the representers are computed, the LM update and covariance assembly reduce to linear algebra in observation space, independently of the discretisation dimension. In 1D, the explicit moving-boundary solution is used to establish posterior well-posedness and existence of MAP estimators, and to derive closed-form Fr\'echet derivatives and representers. In 2D, we introduce a very weak mixed formulation coupling pressure, interface velocity and domain evolution. A formal one-sided directional shape linearisation yields the corresponding linearised state and adjoint systems, with observation-wise representers computed through independent, parallel adjoint problems. Numerical experiments show that the 1D LMAP approximation closely matches a reference MCMC posterior while requiring \((10^1)\) rather than \((10^510^6)\) forward simulations. In 2D, the method produces reconstructions and uncertainty estimates comparable to ensemble Kalman inversion with large ensembles, at substantially lower computational cost. The workflow is demonstrated across several geometries and experimental configurations without reformulating the inversion methodology.
tldr: This paper develops a Bayesian inversion framework for moving boundary Darcy flow, focusing on computational efficiency in parameter estimation.
motivation: The authors aim to efficiently recover spatially varying permeability in resin transfer moulding, a problem with moving boundaries that is computationally challenging.
method: They propose an observation-wise representer formulation, leading to a reduced Levenberg-Marquardt method for MAP estimation and a finite-rank covariance approximation, with parallel adjoint computations.
result: In 1D, the method matches MCMC posteriors with far fewer simulations; in 2D, it provides comparable reconstructions to ensemble Kalman inversion at lower cost.
conclusion: The framework offers a computationally efficient approach to Bayesian inversion in moving boundary flow, with potential for broader applications.

title: Contour Integral Methods And Model Order Reduction For Parametric Linear Control Systems
authors: Mattia Manucci Serkan Gugercin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a contour integral method (CIM) for efficiently computing outputs of parametric linear systems in control form over specified time intervals and to a user-prescribed accuracy. The CIM approximates the inverse Laplace transform via a quadrature rule applied along a modified integration contour. For parametric systems, we show how CIM integrates effectively with projection-based model order reduction (MOR) where a greedy algorithm builds the projection spaces following an error estimate we derive for this setting. We additionally demonstrate that the developed projection framework naturally enforces Hermite interpolation conditions. This combination substantially lowers the cost of evaluating the input-output relations across the parameter domain, for a wide range of input functions, and for initial conditions well captured by a low-dimensional subspace.. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the approach on benchmark non-parametric and parametric control systems, comparing against state-of-the-art projection-based MOR methods.
tldr: This paper introduces a contour integral method combined with model order reduction for efficient simulation of parametric linear control systems.
motivation: The authors aim to reduce the computational cost of evaluating input-output relations of parametric linear systems over time intervals, which is important in control system design and simulation.
method: They approximate the inverse Laplace transform using a quadrature rule on a modified contour, and integrate this with projection-based model order reduction using a greedy algorithm and an error estimate, also enforcing Hermite interpolation.
result: The approach demonstrates accuracy and efficiency on benchmark non-parametric and parametric control systems, outperforming state-of-the-art projection-based MOR methods.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a computationally efficient way to simulate parametric linear control systems, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hyperbolicity And Ergodicity In Randomly Perturbed Billiard Systems
authors: Hong-Kun Zhang Kien Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the Lyapunov exponents and hyperbolicity of random billiard systems under small stochastic perturbations. Our study begins with a review of the necessary theoretical background on Lyapunov exponents for stationary sequences of matrices and Markov processes. We then consider several classical billiard systems and demonstrate that random perturbations can lead to significant changes in their dynamical properties. Specifically, we show that non-circular elliptic and lemon billiards exhibit both ergodicity and hyperbolicity under random perturbations, whereas circular billiards, while ergodic, maintain zero Lyapunov exponents. We also establish conditions under which the largest Lyapunov exponent becomes positive, indicating the emergence of hyperbolic behavior in these systems. These results provide new insights into the stability and chaotic properties of dynamical systems subjected to random noise, with implications for the broader study of smooth dynamical systems.
tldr: This paper studies Lyapunov exponents and hyperbolicity in randomly perturbed billiard systems, a topic in dynamical systems theory.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how random perturbations affect the chaotic properties of classical billiard systems, which is a fundamental question in dynamical systems.
method: They review Lyapunov exponents for stationary sequences and Markov processes, then analyze specific billiard systems (elliptic, lemon, circular) under small stochastic perturbations.
result: They show that non-circular elliptic and lemon billiards become ergodic and hyperbolic under perturbations, while circular billiards remain ergodic with zero Lyapunov exponents. Conditions for positive largest Lyapunov exponent are established.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the stability and chaos of dynamical systems under noise, but the topic is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Splitting Methods For Intermediate Long Wave And Perturbed Benjamin--Ono Models
authors: Yvonne Alama Bronsard, Cl\'ementine Court\`es, Benjamin Melinand
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, novel integrability techniques, and most notably Birkhoff coordinates followed by an explicit formula, have been introduced to solve the Benjamin--Ono (BO) equation, leading to major theoretical and computational advances. We propose to perturb this explicit BO formula via a novel splitting method for numerically solving a class of PDEs, which includes the Intermediate Long Wave (ILW) equation, as well as other quasilinear equations that are not necessarily integrable. Using the Birkhoff coordinates of BO we establish first-order convergence in the [MATH]-norm ([MATH]) while requiring only one additional derivative on the initial data [MATH], significantly improving upon the regularity requirements of typical splitting methods for nonlinear dispersive equations. Furthermore, we prove that in the deep-water limit, the scheme for the ILW equation converges to the BO solution. Computational advantages of these schemes are shown in simulations: unlike classical splitting methods, our approach does not require a restrictive quadratic time step condition to nearly preserve energy over long time scales, thus rendering efficient and accurate long-time simulations feasible. As an application, we numerically explore the soliton resolution conjecture for both the ILW and a KdV--BO equation.
tldr: This paper introduces a novel splitting method for numerically solving the Intermediate Long Wave (ILW) equation and other quasilinear dispersive PDEs, leveraging Birkhoff coordinates of the Benjamin-Ono equation.
motivation: The authors aim to improve numerical methods for nonlinear dispersive equations, specifically the ILW equation, by exploiting recent integrability techniques for the Benjamin-Ono equation to achieve better convergence and long-time stability.
method: They propose a splitting method that perturbs the explicit solution formula for the Benjamin-Ono equation, using Birkhoff coordinates, and prove first-order convergence in a suitable norm with minimal regularity requirements. They also show the scheme converges to the BO solution in the deep-water limit.
result: The method achieves first-order convergence with only one additional derivative on initial data, avoids restrictive time-step conditions for energy preservation, and enables efficient long-time simulations. Numerical experiments explore soliton resolution for ILW and KdV-BO equations.
conclusion: The proposed splitting method offers a computationally efficient and accurate approach for simulating ILW and related equations, with theoretical guarantees and practical advantages over classical methods.

title: Divergence-free Interpolation Of Tangential Vector Fields Via Matrix-valued Kernels
authors: Zhengjie Sun, Lishuo Dong, Biao Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop and analyze a family of divergence-free kernel interpolation methods for tangential vector fields on the unit sphere. Starting from scalar radial kernels in Euclidean space, we construct tangent-valued, surface divergence-free matrix kernels without repeatedly applying surface differential operators. The construction separates the geometric enforcement of the divergence-free constraint from the choice of scalar generator and admits lower-order variants with reduced regularity requirements compared with classical potential-based methods. Using vector spherical harmonics, we derive explicit kernel representations and characterize their Fourier multipliers. We also introduce an inverse Laplace-Beltrami construction that preserves the multipliers of the underlying scalar zonal kernel. For interpolation at scattered nodes, we establish a lower bound for the smallest eigenvalue of the interpolation matrix and derive pointwise and Sobolev error estimates, including superconvergence for targets smoother than the native space. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical convergence and stability results, while additional examples on nonspherical surfaces illustrate the applicability of the kernel formula beyond the sphere.
tldr: This paper develops divergence-free kernel interpolation methods for tangential vector fields on the sphere, with theoretical and numerical analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to construct divergence-free matrix kernels for interpolating tangential vector fields on the sphere, improving on classical methods by separating geometric constraints from scalar generators and offering lower regularity requirements.
method: They construct tangent-valued, surface divergence-free matrix kernels from scalar radial kernels, derive explicit representations using vector spherical harmonics, and introduce an inverse Laplace-Beltrami construction. They also analyze the interpolation matrix spectrum and derive error estimates.
result: They establish lower bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of the interpolation matrix, derive pointwise and Sobolev error estimates including superconvergence, and confirm theoretical results with numerical experiments on the sphere and other surfaces.
conclusion: The proposed methods provide a flexible and theoretically sound framework for divergence-free interpolation on the sphere, with potential extensions to other surfaces.

title: Iterative Decoupling Methods For A Total-Pressure Formulation Of Quasi-Static Electroporoelasticity
authors: Huipeng Gu, Mingchao Cai, Jingzhi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quasi-static electroporoelasticity couples Maxwell's equations with Biot's poroelasticity through electrokinetic coupling between the electric field and the pressure gradient. By introducing the total pressure, the electroporoelasticity equations are reformulated as a five-field system to address poroelastic locking in the nearly incompressible regime. For the resulting five-field system, a monolithic weak formulation is derived, together with a continuous stability estimate. A second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) time discretization and a mixed finite- element spatial discretization are then introduced, yieling to a fully discrete monolithic scheme. Building on this scheme, we develop an iterative decoupling method that alternates between an electromagnetic subproblem and a poroelastic subproblem, and prove its geometric convergence to the monolithic solution with an explicit mesh-independent contraction factor under the physical coupling condition. An algebraically equivalent reduced form is also presented, in which the electromagnetic block is solved only once per time step, while the poroelastic block is solved iteratively with electric-field correction updates obtained from the pressure-gradient feedback. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical predictions and demonstrate the locking-free performance.
tldr: This paper develops iterative decoupling methods for a total-pressure formulation of quasi-static electroporoelasticity, focusing on numerical analysis and locking-free performance.
motivation: The authors aim to address poroelastic locking in the nearly incompressible regime and to develop efficient numerical methods for coupled electroporoelasticity.
method: They reformulate the equations as a five-field system, derive a monolithic weak formulation, and introduce BDF2 time discretization with mixed finite-element spatial discretization. They then propose an iterative decoupling method alternating between electromagnetic and poroelastic subproblems, with a reduced form solving the electromagnetic block once per time step.
result: They prove geometric convergence with an explicit mesh-independent contraction factor under the physical coupling condition, and numerical experiments verify the theoretical predictions and demonstrate locking-free performance.
conclusion: The proposed iterative decoupling methods are efficient and stable for quasi-static electroporoelasticity, providing a robust numerical approach for this coupled problem.

title: Convergence Rates For Variational Inequality Projection Neural Networks With A State-Dependent Metric
authors: Mohammed Alshahrani
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study continuous-time projection neural networks for variational inequalities on closed convex sets. A positive definite matrix that depends on the state preconditions the operator, and its inverse defines the projection metric. Existing convergence analyses of this flow cover Hessian-generated inverse metrics and state-dependent scalar metrics. In the first case, a Bregman distance eliminates metric-derivative terms. We treat a matrix metric whose inverse is of neither kind. We prove joint regularity of the projection in its argument and metric. Under common spectral bounds, the Euclidean Lipschitz estimate improves from the squared bound to the bound itself. For Lipschitz strongly monotone operators and Lipschitz metrics, we prove local exponential convergence with explicit rate and radius. On compact feasible sets, an explicit metric-variation bound yields global exponential convergence. A twice continuously differentiable, uniformly positive definite metric and a strongly monotone linear operator produce an annulus of periodic orbits. The inverse metric violates Hessian integrability throughout the annulus. Deterministic computations confirm the analytic formulas and quantify slack in both convergence certificates.
tldr: This paper analyzes convergence rates for projection neural networks solving variational inequalities with a state-dependent metric, a topic in optimization and neural networks, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to extend convergence analysis of continuous-time projection neural networks to a more general state-dependent metric, addressing a gap in existing theory.
method: The authors prove joint regularity of the projection, derive improved Lipschitz estimates, and establish local and global exponential convergence under spectral bounds and monotonicity assumptions. They also construct an example with periodic orbits.
result: They obtain explicit convergence rates and radii, and demonstrate that the inverse metric can violate Hessian integrability, leading to periodic orbits in a specific case.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous convergence guarantees for a broader class of projection neural networks, but it is purely in the domain of optimization and neural networks, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Nearly Optimal Kolmogorov Widths Under Holomorphic Mappings
authors: Guozhi Zhang Yuwen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes essentially optimal asymptotic bounds for Kolmogorov widths under holomorphic mappings between complex Banach spaces. Given a compact parameter set whose Kolmogorov widths decay algebraically with rate s, we prove that the widths of its image under a holomorphic mapping decay algebraically with every rate t<s, thereby answering an open question raised by Cohen and DeVore. As an application, we obtain a sharp characterization of the approximability of solution manifolds associated with inf-sup stable parametrized PDEs. We also construct an explicit example showing that the arbitrarily small loss in the algebraic decay exponent is unavoidable. Finally, we provide similar characterization of asymptotic bounds for Kolmogorov widths in the exponentially decaying regime. Our analysis involves multilinear Taylor expansion in Banach spaces and a novel block dyadic expansion-truncation technique.
tldr: This paper proves nearly optimal asymptotic bounds for Kolmogorov widths under holomorphic mappings between complex Banach spaces, with applications to parametrized PDEs.
motivation: The paper addresses an open question by Cohen and DeVore regarding the decay of Kolmogorov widths under holomorphic mappings, which is relevant to approximation theory and numerical analysis.
method: The authors use multilinear Taylor expansion in Banach spaces and a novel block dyadic expansion-truncation technique to establish the bounds.
result: They show that if the parameter set has algebraically decaying Kolmogorov widths with rate s, then the image under a holomorphic mapping has widths decaying with any rate t < s, and this loss is unavoidable. They also provide analogous results for exponential decay.
conclusion: The work provides a sharp characterization of approximability for solution manifolds of inf-sup stable parametrized PDEs, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fast Gradient Algorithm With Dry-like Friction And Nonmonotone Line Search For Nonconvex Optimization Problems
authors: Lien T. Nguyen, Andrew Eberhard, Xinghuo Yu, Chaojie Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a fast gradient algorithm for the problem of minimizing a differentiable (possibly nonconvex) function in Hilbert spaces. We first extend the dry friction property for convex functions to what we call the dry-like friction property in a nonconvex setting, and then employ a line search technique to adaptively update parameters at each iteration. Depending on the choice of parameters, the proposed algorithm exhibits subsequential convergence to a critical point or full sequential convergence to an ``approximate'' critical point of the objective function. We also establish the full sequential convergence to a critical point under the Kurdyka--Lojasiewicz (KL) property of a merit function. Thanks to the parameters' flexibility, our algorithm can reduce to a number of existing inertial gradient algorithms with Hessian damping and dry friction. By exploiting variational properties of the Moreau envelope, the proposed algorithm is adapted to address weakly convex nonsmooth optimization problems. In particular, we extend the result on KL exponent for the Moreau envelope of a convex KL function to a broad class of KL functions that are not necessarily convex nor continuous. Simulation results illustrate the efficiency of our algorithm and demonstrate the potential advantages of combining dry-like friction with extrapolation and line search techniques.
tldr: This paper proposes a fast gradient algorithm with dry-like friction and nonmonotone line search for nonconvex optimization, with convergence guarantees under KL property.
motivation: The authors aim to improve convergence of inertial gradient methods for nonconvex problems by extending dry friction to nonconvex settings and using adaptive line search.
method: They introduce a dry-like friction property, employ a nonmonotone line search to update parameters, and analyze subsequential and full sequential convergence, including under KL property. They also adapt the method to weakly convex nonsmooth problems via Moreau envelope.
result: The algorithm achieves subsequential convergence to a critical point or full convergence to an approximate critical point, and full convergence under KL property. Simulations show efficiency.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm generalizes several existing inertial gradient methods and demonstrates advantages of combining dry-like friction with extrapolation and line search.

title: Curvature Residual Geometry In Bregman Regression
authors: Vu Khac Ky
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider linear regression models fitted by minimizing Bregman losses of the form \[ {n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[ \phi(y_i)-\phi(x_i^\top\theta) -\phi'(x_i^\top\theta) \bigl(y_i-x_i^\top\theta\bigr) \right], \] where \(y_i\) is the observed response and \(x_i^\top\theta\) is the linear prediction. Even when the generating potential \(\phi\) is strongly convex, the resulting regression objective may be nonconvex in \(\theta\). This creates a gap between the convexity of the generating potential and the optimization geometry of the fitted model. The Hessian can be written as a weighted Gram matrix whose weights depend on the derivatives of the potential and the current residuals. This representation gives simple conditions for local strong convexity, smoothness, and conditional linear convergence of gradient descent. For the quadratic--quartic potential, we derive an exact scalar convexity condition, identify the interval of negative curvature, and obtain local and global sufficient conditions for positive curvature. Numerical experiments indicate that these scalar conditions may fail while the full Hessian remains positive definite at the evaluated points. They also indicate that the range of tested gradient-descent step sizes leading to convergence decreases as the quartic parameter grows. These results characterize how residual-dependent curvature interacts with the generating potential and the design matrix in reverse Bregman regression.
tldr: This paper analyzes the optimization geometry of Bregman regression, focusing on curvature conditions and convergence of gradient descent.
motivation: The paper addresses a gap between the convexity of the generating potential and the nonconvexity of the regression objective, which is important for understanding optimization in such models.
method: The authors derive conditions for local strong convexity and smoothness by expressing the Hessian as a weighted Gram matrix, and analyze a quadratic-quartic potential to obtain exact scalar convexity conditions.
result: They identify intervals of negative curvature and provide sufficient conditions for positive curvature, with numerical experiments showing that scalar conditions may fail while the full Hessian remains positive definite.
conclusion: The work characterizes how residual-dependent curvature interacts with the potential and design matrix, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quadratic Degree Sequence Optimization And The Critical Roots Of A Graph
authors: Shmuel Onn Fr\'ed\'eric Meunier
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The degree sequence optimization problem is to find a subgraph of a given graph which maximizes the sum over all vertices of a given function evaluated at the subgraph degree of that vertex. Here we study this problem and its complexity for quadratic functions. In particular, we introduce the critical roots of a graph, and show they define intervals over which the optimal value of the problem, as the quadratic root varies, is convex piecewise affine.
tldr: This paper studies the complexity of optimizing quadratic degree sequence functions on graphs, introducing the concept of critical roots.
motivation: The degree sequence optimization problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem with applications in network design and other areas. Understanding its complexity for quadratic functions is of theoretical interest.
method: The authors analyze the problem for quadratic functions, introduce the concept of critical roots of a graph, and study the structure of the optimal value as a function of the quadratic root.
result: They show that the optimal value, as the quadratic root varies, is convex piecewise affine over intervals defined by the critical roots.
conclusion: The paper provides new theoretical insights into the degree sequence optimization problem, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Neural Operator View On U-Nets For Inverse Imaging Problems
authors: Alexander Auras, Martin Burger, Samira Kabri, Michael Moeller, Michael Schopf-Kuester
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks have shown great empirical success in the solution of a wide variety of ill-posed inverse problems in imaging. Yet, very few works have studied their behavior in the limit that turns the discretized ill-conditioned problems into truly ill-posed ones, i.e., for an increasing resolution of the discretization. In this work, we review common approaches to neural operator learning in architectures that resemble a U-Net, one of the most common classical architectures for inverse imaging problems. We discuss advantages and drawbacks of the respective approaches, consider a 1D toy example for improved interpretability, and present extensive numerical experiments on how different types of neural operator U-Nets can improve a first (crude) limited angle CT-reconstruction. In particular, we study how well networks trained for a certain resolution of the discretization generalize to other resolutions. Our finding is that while U-shaped neural operator architectures are by design resolution-invariant, the classical U-Net architecture seems to be more robust with respect to resolution changes than expected.
tldr: This paper studies U-Net architectures for inverse imaging problems from a neural operator perspective, focusing on resolution invariance.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the behavior of deep neural networks for ill-posed inverse problems as discretization resolution increases, which is rarely studied.
method: They review neural operator approaches in U-Net-like architectures, analyze a 1D toy example, and conduct numerical experiments on limited angle CT reconstruction, testing generalization across resolutions.
result: They find that U-shaped neural operator architectures are resolution-invariant by design, but classical U-Nets are more robust to resolution changes than expected.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the design of neural networks for inverse problems, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Post-Hoc Trajectory-Risk Certification For Modular LLM-Based Security Agents
authors: Zhenpeng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous security agents operate as staged pipelines, such as classifying network traffic and then attributing attacks to a specific technique. Split conformal prediction gives each stage finite-sample coverage, but deployment requires a trajectory-level guarantee across the full chain. These guarantees do not compose automatically when stages are independently trained and calibrated. Bonferroni allocation is distribution-free but conservative under correlated errors. We show that a natural pairwise-correlation extension to three or more stages is invalid because it gives a lower rather than an upper bound, and derive a valid spanning-tree alternative. We distinguish whether stages are dependent from whether an audit sample is large enough to certify that dependence, and give matching upper and information-theoretic lower sample-complexity bounds. We also show that coarse-to-fine label selection can create near-perfect measured correlation without learned dependence. On a two-stage intrusion-detection pipeline across 6 open LLMs and 2 datasets, removing this artifact reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0-0.78. A direct audit of trajectory failure becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni once the audit reaches the required sample size, but is worse when undersized. A modular certificate using per-stage certificates and a pairwise overlap bound yields a positive average gain of 0.6%, quantifying the cost of lacking joint access. Same-model, cross-model, and permuted-pairing tests show that residual dependence reflects shared sample difficulty, not shared model representations. Average trajectory coverage across 12 configurations is 92.7% +/- 2.4% at alpha = 0.10. Under cross-dataset deployment, single-step miscoverage reaches 100% even when accuracy remains 78%, showing that distribution shift destroys calibrated confidence before raw accuracy.
tldr: This paper proposes a method for certifying trajectory-level risk in modular LLM-based security agents using conformal prediction and spanning-tree correlation bounds.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of providing finite-sample coverage guarantees for multi-stage security pipelines, where per-stage guarantees do not compose automatically.
method: The authors derive a valid spanning-tree alternative to Bonferroni allocation for correlated errors, and provide sample-complexity bounds and a modular certificate using per-stage certificates and pairwise overlap bounds.
result: Experiments on intrusion-detection pipelines show that removing correlation artifacts reduces measured correlation from near 1 to 0-0.78, and the direct audit becomes 13.7% tighter than Bonferroni when adequately sized, while modular certificates yield a small positive gain.
conclusion: The work highlights the impact of distribution shift on calibrated confidence and provides a method for trajectory-level certification, but it is not aligned with the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: A Survey Of Adversarial Efficiency Degradation For Vision Transformer By Exploiting Input-adaptive Optimization
authors: Anadi Goyal, Nandish Chattopadhyay, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Chandan Karfa
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) increasingly rely on input-adaptive inference, such as token pruning and early halting, to meet energy and latency budgets. This survey examines a recent class of adversarial efficiency degradation attacks that target these mechanisms to increase computation without necessarily degrading accuracy. We unify and compare two representative attacks, SlowFormer (a universal adversarial patch) and DeSparsify (per-image perturbations), across three popular token-pruning frameworks: A-ViT, ATS, and AdaViT. We standardize reporting using GFLOPs, accuracy loss, and an Attack Success (AS) metric that measures how much of the model's compute savings the attack takes away. Understanding these attacks is crucial for designing countermeasures that not only mitigate risk but also remain lightweight, since deployment often occurs in low-power settings such as mobile or embedded devices. To organize our analysis, we focus on three questions: how input-adaptive optimizations (e.g., token pruning and early halting) create attack surfaces for efficiency degradation; how such attacks operate in practice and which optimizations are most vulnerable; and which defenses exist today and whether they meaningfully restore efficiency under attack.
tldr: A survey of adversarial attacks that degrade the efficiency of Vision Transformers by exploiting input-adaptive inference mechanisms.
motivation: To understand and mitigate security vulnerabilities in efficient ViT inference, which is critical for low-power deployment.
method: Unifies and compares two attacks (SlowFormer and DeSparsify) across three token-pruning frameworks, standardizing metrics like GFLOPs and Attack Success.
result: Identifies which optimizations are most vulnerable and evaluates existing defenses.
conclusion: Highlights the need for lightweight countermeasures to restore efficiency under attack.

title: PromptShield Home: Ambient Multimodal Prompt Injection Defense For Smart-Home Agents
authors: He Zhang, Feilong Li, Dingning Long, Yilin Cui, Peijun Zhang, Yuewen Zhang, Qianyao Xu, Xinyi Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart-home assistants increasingly use multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that perceive video and audio directly. This raises a safety question specific to the home: can the agent tell a genuine user command from ambient or externally-sourced content, television speech, on-screen text, or an overheard conversation, that merely looks like a command? We introduce PromptShield-Home, a pilot benchmark of realistic smart-home scenarios spanning addressee ambiguity, screen/audio injection, health-monitor false triggers, mixed occupancy, and a legitimate-command floor, and use it to compare three abstraction layers: traditional detectors (L0), a single MLLM agent (L1; vision, vision+ASR, and audio-visual), and multi-agent mediation (L2; voting, role specialists, cross-model arbitration). Because the label distribution is skewed toward inaction, aggregate accuracy is misleading, a constant always-block predictor scores 82%, so we report unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately. The two paradigms fail in opposite ways: detectors act on everything, while every MLLM configuration over-refuses, completing almost no genuine command and missing a true fall in every case. Crucially, their correct sets are disjoint: an oracle that always picks the right layer reaches 94.1%, against 76.5% for the best single layer. We report this as an upper bound, not a system - no router is implemented - and argue that home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for detecting prompt injection attacks in smart-home agents using multimodal LLMs, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Smart-home agents using multimodal LLMs may be vulnerable to ambient prompt injection attacks, where commands from TV or other sources are mistaken for user commands. The authors aim to evaluate different abstraction layers for defense.
method: They create a benchmark with realistic scenarios and compare traditional detectors, a single MLLM agent, and multi-agent mediation, reporting unsafe-execution and safe-completion rates separately.
result: Detectors act on everything while MLLMs over-refuse, and their correct sets are disjoint, with an oracle achieving 94.1% versus 76.5% for the best single layer.
conclusion: Home-agent safety is best served by learned routing and sensor fusion, not by replacing detectors with an MLLM.

title: A Bitopological Approach To Finite Reduction And Bounded Exact-Value Certificates For Fitting's Finite Heyting-valued Modal Logic
authors: Litan Kumar Das, Kumar Sankar Ray, Prakash Chandra Mali
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fitting's finite Heyting-valued modal logic interprets modal formulas over a finite Heyting algebra. We use a relational bitopological representation to obtain a finite-state reduction. For a finite model and a finite vocabulary, the modal subalgebra generated by the atomic valuations determines a state-evaluation map. We prove that the observational quotient is isomorphic to its finite image in the bitopological dual and that the quotient relation is the restriction of the canonical dual relation. Hence every formula over the vocabulary preserves its exact truth value, and the quotient is minimal among surjective reductions through which all generated observations factor. In addition, for any formula and state, we construct a finite tree-like exact-value certificate whose depth is bounded by modal depth and whose branching depends only on the height of the truth-value algebra and the number of boxed subformulas. Failed formulas therefore admit bounded reduced counterexamples preserving their precise failure values.
tldr: This paper presents a bitopological approach to finite reduction and bounded exact-value certificates for Fitting's finite Heyting-valued modal logic.
motivation: The research interests focus on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems; this paper is in mathematical logic and modal logic, which is outside these areas.
method: The authors use a relational bitopological representation to obtain a finite-state reduction and construct finite tree-like exact-value certificates for formulas.
result: They prove that the observational quotient is isomorphic to its finite image in the bitopological dual, and that every formula preserves its exact truth value, with bounded certificates for failed formulas.
conclusion: The paper contributes to the theory of Heyting-valued modal logic but has no connection to the specified research directions.

title: Predictor-Impossibility Theorem And Applications
authors: Tom Altman
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a hierarchy consisting of stage machines, stage domains, and stage languages generated by semantic operators. The central result is a Predictor Impossibility Theorem (PITT), which shows that no effective predictor family can uniformly determine all stage languages of our hierarchy. The proof makes use of a pseudo-complement construction to obtain a language that yields a contradiction with every language in P. We then define an aggregate language MIS and establish a formal Slice Theorem connecting aggregate inputs to individual stage languages. This provides a rigorous Bridge Theorem from polynomial-time decidability of MIS to the existence of an effective predictor family. By utilizing succinct representations, the aggregate language is shown to be undecidable in deterministic polynomial time. Under the aggregate growth condition defining valid aggregate objects, MIS is shown to belong to NP. Combining these two results yields our main theorem: MIS in NP setminus P. The paper is organized so that PITT stands independently as a theoretic result, while the complexity-theoretic consequences are derived from the aggregate-language framework. The method does not relativize, algebrize, or naturalize.
tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchy of stage languages and proves a Predictor Impossibility Theorem, leading to a claim that MIS is in NP but not P, which is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to establish a fundamental impossibility result about predictors and to prove a separation between NP and P using a novel aggregate language framework.
method: The method involves defining stage machines, stage domains, and stage languages via semantic operators, using a pseudo-complement construction to prove the Predictor Impossibility Theorem, and then constructing an aggregate language MIS with a Slice Theorem to connect its decidability to the existence of effective predictors.
result: The main result is that MIS is in NP but not in P, implying P ≠ NP, under the assumption that the aggregate growth condition holds.
conclusion: The paper concludes that the Predictor Impossibility Theorem stands independently, and the complexity-theoretic consequences follow from the aggregate-language framework, with the method not relativizing, algebrizing, or naturalizing.

title: Abc: Numerical Data Collection Under Local Differential Privacy Without Prior Knowledge
authors: Incheol Baek, Hyungbin Kim, Yon Dohn Chung
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local Differential Privacy (LDP) provides strong privacy guarantees for collecting numerical data. A fundamental challenge, however, is that existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown in practice. This lack of prior knowledge creates a critical dilemma for the data collector: if the chosen domain is too narrow, values outside the range are clipped, leading to information loss. Conversely, if the domain is too wide, excessive noise is added during the privatization process, which degrades the quality of collected data. This highlights the need for methods that can dynamically estimate the data domain. In this work, we propose an adaptive LDP framework that addresses this problem. In our method, each user sends two pieces of information: their perturbed numerical data, and a privatized signal indicating if their original value was clipped by the current domain. By aggregating these signals, our proposed method, Adaptive Bounding of Clipping regions (ABC) method, iteratively adjusts the domain to fit the underlying data distribution without prior knowledge. Our theoretical analysis shows that the estimated data domain converges to an appropriate range. In the empirical evaluation, the results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves the quality of numerical data collection across various datasets and underlying LDP mechanisms. We also show that the estimated range successfully converges in practice and our approach is robust to its hyperparameters through comprehensive ablation studies.
tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive local differential privacy framework for numerical data collection without prior knowledge of the data domain.
motivation: Existing LDP mechanisms require a predefined data domain, which is often unknown, leading to information loss or excessive noise.
method: The method, ABC, has each user send perturbed data and a privatized clipping signal, which are aggregated to iteratively adjust the domain.
result: Theoretical analysis shows convergence of the estimated domain, and empirical evaluations demonstrate improved data quality across datasets and mechanisms.
conclusion: The adaptive domain estimation approach effectively addresses the unknown domain problem in LDP numerical data collection.

title: Tool Demo: Topology Analysis With Gpml For Detection Of Cyberattacks In Water Distribution Networks
authors: Majed Jaber (icube-R\'eseaux), Abdul Qadir Khan (LRE, Icube), Ankush Meshram (LRE, Icube), Julien Michel (LRE, Icube), C\^ome Frapp\'e - - Vialatoux (icube, LRE), Pierre Parrend
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Water distribution networks depends on industrial control systems to integrate the physical process with communication network, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks that alter the traffic pattern and network behavior. Traditional detection approaches that rely on raw traffic or protocol information often oversee structural changes that are induced by such attacks. In this work, we presents a topology-driven approach for detection of cyberattacks in water distribution networks based on Graph Processing for Machine Learning (GPML) framework. The raw traffic is transformed into dynamic graphs, from which community and spectral metrics are extracted and analyzed for any structural and communication modifications with time. The proposed methodology is evaluated on three industrial water distribution datasets such as HITL, SWaT, and CrossTest. Spectral and community graph metrics improve the model performance in detection of cyber and pyhiscal attacks across the three datasets.
tldr: This paper applies graph-based machine learning to detect cyberattacks in water distribution networks, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: Water distribution networks are vulnerable to cyberattacks, and traditional detection methods miss structural changes. The authors aim to use topology analysis to improve detection.
method: They transform raw network traffic into dynamic graphs and extract community and spectral metrics using the GPML framework, then analyze these metrics over time to detect anomalies.
result: The proposed method improves detection of cyber and physical attacks across three industrial datasets (HITL, SWaT, CrossTest).
conclusion: Topology-driven analysis with graph metrics is effective for detecting attacks in water distribution networks, but the topic is outside the scope of the user's research interests.

title: MMAligner: Safeguarding Multimodal Large Language Models Through Representation Calibration
authors: Shenyi Zhang, Keyan Guo, Zihao Wang, Xuebin Li, Lingchen Zhao, Hongxin Hu, Chao Shen, Qian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often refuse unsafe text prompts yet generate harmful responses to semantically equivalent multimodal inputs. Existing defenses either rely on external guardrails, which add inference overhead without repairing intrinsic flaws, or safety fine-tuning, which treats alignment as black-box optimization and may sacrifice utility or require large multimodal datasets. To identify the cause of this safety disparity, we analyze MLLM representations geometrically. We find that safety mechanisms learned from text persist across modalities: a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary remain effective, and representations inside this boundary consistently trigger refusals. However, unsafe multimodal inputs undergo a representation shift that places most of them outside the boundary, allowing them to bypass the model's intrinsic safety mechanism. This indicates that multimodal safety degradation stems from representation misalignment rather than the absence of safety capability. Based on this finding, we propose MMAligner, a safeguarding method that calibrates unsafe multimodal representations into the pre-existing refusal region. MMAligner applies a hard lower bound to ensure refusal, a soft upper bound to avoid excessive modification, and a preservation objective for benign inputs. Experiments across multiple open-source MLLMs show that MMAligner raises the average refusal rate on unsafe multimodal inputs to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation and minimal training data, substantially improving the safety-utility trade-off over existing baselines. (*Due to the notification from arXiv, "The Abstract field cannot be longer than 1,920 characters", the Abstract that appeared is shortened.).
tldr: This paper proposes MMAligner, a method to calibrate multimodal large language model representations to improve safety against harmful multimodal inputs.
motivation: Multimodal LLMs can be tricked into generating harmful responses despite safety training on text, due to representation misalignment across modalities.
method: MMAligner identifies a shared safety subspace and refusal boundary, then applies hard and soft bounds to calibrate unsafe multimodal representations into the refusal region while preserving benign inputs.
result: Experiments show MMAligner raises refusal rates to 99% with less than 2% utility degradation across multiple open-source MLLMs.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that safety degradation in MLLMs stems from representation misalignment and can be fixed with minimal training data.

title: Some Generalizations Of The Bridge And Torch Problem
authors: Gerard Sayson Pang Ern Thang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.05190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the classic bridge and torch problem with crossing times [MATH], we derive a closed-form expression for the optimal crossing time [MATH] using a recurrence relation derived from the problem's optimal substructure, thus obtaining \[T\left(n\right)={4}+3n-5+{8}\] which holds for all [MATH]. We generalize the problem to a bridge of capacity 3 and obtain the optimal crossing time \[T_3\left(n\right)=}{6}+2n-{36}+}{4}-{9}\cos\left({3}\right)\] which holds for all [MATH]. As such, we obtain a new sequence A392834 in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. Lastly, we also explore this problem for star graphs, and see how we can recover some classic identities involving the sum of floor functions.
tldr: This paper derives closed-form solutions for the bridge and torch problem and its generalizations, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to solve a classic combinatorial optimization problem and its variants, providing mathematical formulas and new integer sequences.
method: The authors use recurrence relations and optimal substructure to derive closed-form expressions for optimal crossing times, and explore generalizations to capacity 3 and star graphs.
result: They obtain closed-form expressions for the optimal crossing time for the classic problem and its capacity-3 generalization, and introduce a new integer sequence A392834.
